seq: The Deepwater Horizon was a floating drilling rig, owned by Transocean and hired by BP.

Below it lay about five thousand feet of water. A pipe called the riser ran down to the seafloor, to the blowout preventer: a three-hundred-sixty-ton stack of valves and steel blades on top of the well. From there, the well went down another two and a half miles into the rock.
The well was about thirty-eight days behind schedule and some fifty-eight million dollars over budget. In an email that April, a BP engineer called it a nightmare well.

A hundred and twenty-six people from thirteen companies were aboard. BP's well site leaders were Bob Kaluza and Don Vidrine. On the drill floor that evening were Transocean's toolpusher Jason Anderson and driller Dewey Revette.
Halliburton had cemented the bottom of the well just after midnight. The plan now was to seal it temporarily, and move the rig on.
Three things stood between the oil and gas in the rock and the rig above: the heavy drilling mud that filled the well, the cement at the bottom, and the blowout preventer.
To leave, the crew would replace the mud in the riser and the top of the well with much lighter seawater. After that, the cement at the bottom would have to hold back the reservoir on its own.
That morning, BP had sent home a team that could have checked the cement. Its decision plan said the check was not needed. The commission later concluded that BP should have run it.
There was a warning in the laboratory, too. Halliburton's own tests had shown the cement mix to be unstable.

The cement would be checked instead with a negative pressure test: lower the pressure inside the well, as if the rig had already gone. If the cement held, nothing would come back: no pressure, and no flow.
There was no standard procedure for running or reading this test. And BP and Transocean had not formally trained their people to do it.
Starting around five p.m., the crew bled the pressure off the drill pipe. It came back. After repeated attempts, it built up to fourteen hundred psi.

They discussed the readings on the rig floor. According to statements from both well site leaders, Jason Anderson said the pressure came from a so-called bladder effect: heavy mud in the riser pressing down on a closed preventer, and pushing pressure into the drill pipe.

Anderson died that night and never gave his own account. A federal court later found that no such effect is known to exist in this kind of test, and questioned whether the idea had come from him at all.

Don Vidrine insisted on repeating the test on the kill line, a narrow pipe from the rig down to the blowout preventer. Nothing flowed from it for thirty minutes. The drill pipe still read fourteen hundred.
Around eight p.m., the test was declared a success.
The commission later wrote that the pressure data were not ambiguous. In its view, the men had started from the assumption that the well could not be flowing.
Four months earlier, a Transocean rig in the North Sea had a near miss after a negative test was declared a success. According to Transocean, the lessons never reached the Deepwater Horizon crew.
At eight-oh-two, the crew began pumping the mud out and seawater in. Halliburton cementer Chris Haire was told the test was good, and to get ready for the final cement plug.

As the heavy mud left the well, so did the weight holding back the reservoir. The cement at the bottom, investigators later concluded, was not holding. According to later computer models, at about eight-fifty, oil and gas began to enter the well.

At nine-oh-one, the drill pipe pressure began to rise while the pumps ran steadily. Minutes later, with the pumps off, fluid kept flowing out. At about nine-ten, the returns were sent overboard, past the meters that measured them.
The crew was busy with other work at the same time. Investigators concluded that the signs were missed.

Around nine-twenty, senior toolpusher Randy Ezell phoned Jason Anderson on the rig floor. By Ezell's account, Anderson told him the test had gone fine: they had watched it for thirty minutes, with no flow.
At about nine-thirty, driller Dewey Revette noticed a pressure difference, and the pumps were shut down. Ten minutes later, mud shot out of the riser onto the rig floor.

Gas was already above the blowout preventer, rising and expanding up the riser. The crew sent the flow to a mud-gas separator on the rig, rather than overboard, and closed the preventer. The separator was not built for a blowout. Gas spread over the rig.
Crane operator Micah Sandell saw mud shooting all the way up the derrick, and then an explosion.
Mike Williams was in his shop, below the rig floor.
He heard alarms beeping from the engine control room next door. Gas had reached the engines.
Williams told investigators he never heard the general alarm.
Investigators found that the general alarm came minutes after the first gas alarms. Dynamic positioning officer Andrea Fleytas sent a Mayday.
Two lifeboats left from the front of the rig. Others were cut off, and jumped fifty to seventy feet into the water. Williams stayed with a group trying to launch a life raft.
The rescue boat had come from the Bankston. Its crew had backed the vessel away from the rig and launched the boat to pull people from the water.
Andrea Fleytas, the officer who had sent the Mayday.

All a hundred and fifteen survivors ended up on the Bankston. The first Coast Guard helicopter arrived a little after eleven p.m. Through the night, the most badly injured were lifted off and flown to shore.
At the muster, eleven men were missing. The Coast Guard searched for three days. They were never found.

In the minutes after the explosions, subsea supervisor Chris Pleasant pressed the emergency disconnect on the bridge. It should have closed the blowout preventer's blind shear ram, the blades meant to cut the drill pipe and seal the well, and freed the rig from the riser. The lights on the panel changed. The rig did not disconnect.

The preventer also had an automatic backup, called the deadman, meant to close the blades on its own if power, communication, and hydraulic pressure from the rig were lost. After the explosions, they were.

Investigators did not fully agree on what happened next. The Chemical Safety Board concluded that the deadman most likely did fire that night, but that the drill pipe inside had buckled and been pushed off center. The blades caught the pipe at its edge, and could not seal the well.
The forensic examination for the federal joint investigation also found the pipe off center, but concluded that the blades most likely closed two days later, when an underwater robot triggered them.
And by the time the crew closed the preventer, the commission noted, the flow may already have been too strong to stop. Earlier detection would have improved the odds.
The blowout preventer was raised from the seafloor in September twenty ten, and taken as evidence.
The Deepwater Horizon burned for about thirty-six hours. On the morning of April twenty-second, it sank.
Oil flowed from the well for eighty-seven days. The government estimated that four point nine million barrels were released. A federal court later put the amount at about four million barrels.
A capping stack stopped the flow on July fifteenth. On September nineteenth, after a relief well, the well was declared permanently sealed.

BP pleaded guilty to fourteen criminal counts, including eleven counts of seaman's manslaughter, and agreed to pay four billion dollars in that case. A federal court later found it grossly negligent. Transocean pleaded guilty to a Clean Water Act violation.
The federal agency that had overseen offshore drilling was broken up. New rules for blowout preventers and well control followed in twenty sixteen.

So why was the well judged safe? Because the test that should have caught the problem was read as a success, with no standard for reading it, and with an explanation that was later found to have no basis. In fact, investigators concluded, the cement at the bottom had failed.
And why didn't the blowout preventer stop it? The signs were missed until gas was already above it. When its blades closed, the drill pipe was in the wrong place for them to seal the well.
The commission traced the disaster to a series of mistakes by BP, Halliburton, and Transocean, and to failures of management. It also wrote that the exact part each mistake played may never be known.
